content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a guideline on syphilis screening and treatment specifically for pregnant women. This document, copyrighted in 2017, allows for non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guideline emphasizes that sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including syphilis, are a significant global public health issue, causing substantial morbidity and mortality. Syphilis, caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, is transmitted through sexual contact, blood transfusion, or transplacentally from a pregnant woman to her fetus. Congenital syphilis, resulting from mother-to-child transmission, can have devastating effects on the fetus if maternal infection is not detected and treated early in pregnancy. In 2012, syphilis was estimated to cause 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes globally, including stillbirths, neonatal deaths, preterm births, and infected infants. The guideline highlights the importance of early detection and treatment of syphilis during pregnancy, ideally before the second trimester, to minimize adverse outcomes. Screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first antenatal care visit is recommended in many countries and is being rapidly scaled up in regions committed to eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis. Serologic tests, such as TPPA and TPHA, are commonly used for syphilis screening and diagnosis. The guideline provides updated recommendations for syphilis screening and treatment in pregnant women, based on the latest evidence and available diagnostic tests. These recommendations are aligned with the 2016 WHO guidelines for the treatment of Treponema pallidum and include links to additional resources for managing congenital syphilis. The document is part of a series of STI-specific guideline modules, which also cover other infections like chlamydia, gonorrhea, and genital herpes. These modules are interconnected and will eventually be consolidated into comprehensive STI guidelines. Countries are strongly encouraged to incorporate updated global guidance into their national protocols, adapting them to local epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility data. The objectives of the guideline are to provide evidence-based recommendations for syphilis screening and treatment in pregnant women and to support countries in updating their national guidelines accordingly. The guideline was developed using the methods outlined in the 2014 WHO handbook for guideline development. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included international STI experts, clinicians, researchers, and program managers. Systematic reviews of the literature were conducted to assess the diagnostic accuracy and effectiveness of various syphilis screening and treatment strategies. Cost-effectiveness analyses were also used to inform the recommendations. The evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, and conflicts of interest were managed according to WHO policies. The recommendations address syphilis screening strategies in different care settings, the optimal sequence of tests, and subsequent treatment. They emphasize the importance of early and adequate treatment to prevent adverse pregnancy outcomes. The guideline also includes recommendations for managing congenital syphilis, providing a comprehensive approach to the care of pregnant women and their infants. The preparation and printing of the guideline were funded exclusively by the UNDP/UNFPA/UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development, and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP). No external funding sources were solicited or used. The guideline acknowledges the contributions of various experts, review groups, and WHO staff involved in its development.
